85.title: Socrates' last day
85.hook: Athens, 399 BCE: he spends his final hours talking with friends about the soul (Plato, Phaedo)
85.tomorrow: I know that I don't know
85.howItsDone: Students of philosophy often meet Socrates in the Phaedo, and his calm, questioning last day is often held up as a picture of facing death with a clear mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the raft: for crossing over, not for carrying on your head. Your line was leave the raft.

If you knew it was your last day, how would you spend it? People answer fast at parties: a beach, a big meal, calling everyone you love. In Athens, a man past seventy actually knew. And he spent it doing exactly what he'd done every other day of his life: talking with his friends, and asking questions. He opens a new week, a week of ordinary saints: not kings or prophets, just people who lived their questions all the way through.
screen: `IF IT WERE YOUR LAST DAY.` → `ATHENS, A PRISON CELL.` → `A WEEK OF ORDINARY SAINTS.`

segments.voice: Socrates had been put on trial by his own city, charged with not honoring the city's gods and with corrupting the young. A jury of Athenians found him guilty and sentenced him to death. But a sacred ship had just sailed to the island of Delos, and by custom no one could be executed until it came back. So he waited in prison a long while, and his friends came every day. His student Plato wrote about the last of those days in the Phaedo, told in the voice of a friend who was there. And Plato lets that friend mention, in passing, that Plato himself was absent: ill, he believes. So it's a story written by a friend, about what other friends saw. That morning the chains come off. Socrates rubs his leg and remarks how pleasure and pain seem joined together; Aesop, he adds, could have made a fable of it. He'd even been turning Aesop's fables into verse in his cell. Then, all day, he talks with his friends about the soul, and whether it survives death. Two of them, Simmias and Cebes, raise hard objections, and Socrates doesn't get defensive. He welcomes them. Don't agree with me to be kind, he tells them, more or less; follow the argument. At sunset he bathes, says goodbye to his family, and calmly drinks the poison the city has prepared. His last words are a small, strange request to his friend Crito: to pay a debt, a rooster owed to the god of healing. People still argue about what that meant. What stays is the picture: with hours left, he wasn't settling things. He was still asking, and still glad to be asked.
screen: `THE TRIAL AND THE SACRED SHIP.` · `PLATO WASN'T THERE; HE WAS ILL.` · `A LAST DAY OF HARD QUESTIONS.` · `THE CUP AT SUNSET.` · then, large: `KEEP ASKING.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you'll probably talk to soon, not the easiest person and not the hardest, and one real question you could ask them: not about logistics, but what they think, or what they've been wondering lately. Picture asking it, and listening to the answer without rushing to agree or correct. Socrates' friends disagreed with him on his last day, and he was glad.
Socrates. A whole final day spent in conversation about the soul, welcoming hard questions, until the sunset.
Your line: keep asking. His very last day was a day of questions. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 85 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: I KNOW THAT I DON'T KNOW.`

86.title: I know that I don't know
86.hook: the oracle calls Socrates wisest, and he decides it's because he knows he doesn't know (Plato, Apology 21)
86.howItsDone: Philosophy classes often begin with Socrates' reading of the oracle, and his habit of testing what people claim to know gave its name to the Socratic method.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Socrates: a whole last day of hard questions, welcomed. Your line was keep asking.

In a meeting, someone asks a question. There's a small pause, then someone answers confidently, and later it turns out they were guessing. Online, everyone has a take on everything within the hour. Even among friends, it can feel like losing to say three little words, so they rarely get said: I don't know. Today goes back, long before yesterday's prison, to the reason Socrates became Socrates. It starts with a friend's trip to the oracle at Delphi, and a very bold question.
screen: `A PAUSE, THEN A CONFIDENT GUESS.` → `A TAKE ON EVERYTHING.` → `A QUESTION FOR THE ORACLE.`

segments.voice: It's in Plato's Apology, his version of the speech Socrates gave at his trial. Socrates tells the jury that his friend Chaerephon, an excitable man, once went to the oracle of Apollo at Delphi and asked: is anyone wiser than Socrates? The priestess answered: no one. Socrates says this baffled him. He knew he wasn't wise, but a god doesn't lie. So he set out to test it. He questioned a politician with a great reputation for wisdom, and found the man thought he knew a great deal, and didn't. Socrates walked away thinking, more or less: I'm a little wiser than him in this one small way. Neither of us knows anything very fine and good, but he thinks he knows, and I don't think I know. Then he tried the poets, who wrote beautiful things but couldn't explain them. Then the craftsmen, who really did know their crafts, but assumed that made them experts on everything else too. So he concluded the oracle meant something humbling: human wisdom is worth little, and the wisest person is the one who knows it. Here's a surprise. The famous line, I know that I know nothing, isn't in Plato in those words. It's a later summary. What Socrates claims is smaller and more precise: I don't think I know what I don't know. And it cost him. Showing important people what they didn't know made him enemies, and helped lead to that trial. But it also made him someone you could actually learn from. You can't learn anything you already think you know.
screen: `IS ANYONE WISER THAN SOCRATES?` · `POLITICIANS, POETS, CRAFTSMEN.` · `HE THINKS HE KNOWS; I DON'T.` · `NOT QUITE THE FAMOUS LINE.` · then, large: `I DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you have a strong opinion about but haven't looked into much, and notice how sure you feel. Then ask it the way Socrates would: how do I actually know that, and what would I need to see to be sure? Let a little space open where the certainty was; it can feel uncomfortable, even a little free.
Oracle. The Delphic oracle that called Socrates wisest, which he read to mean: the wisest person knows they don't know what they don't.
Your line: I don't know. Three small words that take some nerve. Eighty-six days now.

87.title: Brother Lawrence in the kitchen
87.hook: a lay brother finds as much of God among the pots as in the chapel (The Practice of the Presence of God)
87.howItsDone: Many Christians, Catholic and Protestant, read The Practice of the Presence of God and try to keep a quiet, continual conversation with God through ordinary work, as Brother Lawrence described.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the oracle, and Socrates, wise only in not thinking he knew what he didn't. Your line was I don't know.

Picture the sink after a big family dinner. Grease on the pans, somebody's glass with a lipstick mark, the dishwasher already full. It's the least spiritual place in the house. The deep stuff, it seems, happens somewhere else: on a retreat, on a mountain, in a quiet room with a candle. Dishes are what you get through to get back to real life. In the sixteen hundreds, in Paris, a clumsy, cheerful lay brother spent fifteen years in a monastery kitchen and came to the opposite conclusion.
screen: `THE SINK AFTER DINNER.` → `THE DEEP STUFF IS ELSEWHERE?` → `FIFTEEN YEARS AMONG THE POTS.`

segments.voice: His name was Nicolas Herman. He'd been a soldier, wounded in war. The story he told later is that at eighteen, looking at a bare tree in winter, he realized its leaves would come back in spring, and felt, all at once, how much he was held by God. Years later he joined the Discalced Carmelites in Paris, not as a priest but as a lay brother, the kind who did the physical work. He took the name Brother Lawrence, and they put him in the kitchen. By his own account, he didn't like kitchen work, and wasn't especially good at it. He also found the formal methods of prayer hard. So he did something simpler. He decided to do each small thing for the love of God, and to keep talking to God, quietly, all day, as if to a friend in the room. Turning a little omelette in the pan. Picking up a piece of straw from the floor. After he died, a priest who had talked with him collected his conversations and letters into a small book, The Practice of the Presence of God. In it, Lawrence says work time was no different for him from prayer time. In the noise and clatter of his kitchen, with several people calling for different things at once, he felt as close to God as if he were on his knees in chapel. Catholics treasure the book, and many Protestants and people of other paths read it too. You needn't share his faith to borrow the move. The sink doesn't need to be escaped. It can be the place.
screen: `A SOLDIER, A BARE TREE IN WINTER.` · `A LAY BROTHER IN THE KITCHEN.` · `EACH SMALL THING FOR LOVE.` · `WORK TIME, PRAYER TIME: THE SAME.` · then, large: `THE KITCHEN IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: If you're near a sink, a counter or a table, wash one cup, wipe one surface or fold one towel; if not, picture it. Do it slowly, and for someone: whoever will use the cup next, the people you share the space with, anyone you love. If you pray, offer it as Lawrence did, a small thing done with love; if not, just do it completely.
Brother Lawrence. The lay brother who found God as near among the pots and the clatter as in the chapel.
Your line: the kitchen is enough. Small things, done with love, count too. Day eighty-seven.

88.title: The hazelnut
88.hook: Julian of Norwich sees all that is made as small as a hazelnut in her palm, lasting because it is loved (Revelations of Divine Love 5)
88.howItsDone: Christians of many churches read Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love as a classic of prayer, and some church calendars, Anglican ones among them, remember her in May.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brother Lawrence, turning the omelette for love. Your line was the kitchen is enough.

There's a photo of Earth taken from far out in space: a tiny pale dot, almost lost in a beam of light. Everything is on there. Everyone who ever lived. Every war, every wedding, every lunch. And it's so small. Long before any camera left the planet, a woman in England, very sick and close to death, saw something like that, except it was sitting in the palm of her hand.
screen: `A PALE DOT IN SPACE.` → `EVERYTHING, AND SO SMALL.` → `SOMETHING IN HER PALM.`

segments.voice: In May of 1373, a woman in Norwich, in England, was thirty and a half years old and so ill that everyone expected her to die. A priest held a crucifix in front of her eyes. Over the next hours she received what she called sixteen showings, visions about the love of God. She recovered, and wrote the showings down. By her own account, she was still being taught what one of them meant close to twenty years later. The book is called Revelations of Divine Love. Her own name isn't known for certain. Tradition says she lived as an anchoress, in a small room attached to the church of Saint Julian in Norwich, and she's remembered as Julian after that church. Early in the book, she says she was shown a little thing, the size of a hazelnut, lying in the palm of her hand, round as a ball. She looked at it and wondered what it could be. The answer came, in Grace Warrack's old translation: "It is all that is made." The whole created world, in one palm. She marveled how it could last; it seemed so small it might just fall into nothing. And she understood: it lasts, and always will, because God loves it. She saw three things in that little ball: God made it, God loves it, God keeps it. Christians who read Julian often come back to this picture. For anyone, it's a way of looking at small things. A stone, a cup, a hand. Small enough to fall into nothing. Still here.
screen: `NORWICH, MAY 1373.` · `SIXTEEN SHOWINGS.` · `A HAZELNUT IN HER PALM.` · `MADE, LOVED, KEPT.` · then, large: `ALL THAT IS MADE.`

segments.voice: Pick up something small near you, a coin, a button, a pebble, a nut, a ring, or if there's nothing, look at your own open palm. Look at it longer than feels normal: its color, its edges, its weight, how easily it could be lost, and that it's here anyway. If you pray, you can hold Julian's three words: made, loved, kept.
The hazelnut. Julian's vision of everything that is made, small enough to sit in her palm, lasting because it is loved.
Your line: all that is made. Small as it is, it lasts. See you at day eighty-nine.

89.title: Francis and the wolf
89.hook: Francis makes peace between the town of Gubbio and a hungry wolf (Little Flowers of St Francis 21)
89.howItsDone: Catholics and many other Christians honor Francis of Assisi as a saint of peace and of creation; on or near his feast day, October 4, many churches bless animals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hazelnut: Julian's vision of all that is made, small in her palm and loved. Your line was all that is made.

Every town has a wolf. Maybe not a real one: the neighbor everyone avoids, the kid at school who bites back, the relative who ruins every holiday dinner. The usual answer is walls, avoidance, maybe a group chat to complain in. In the old story, the Italian hill town of Gubbio had a real wolf, big and hungry, and the townspeople had stopped leaving the walls without weapons. Then Francis of Assisi walked out of the gate toward it, though they told him not to.
screen: `EVERY TOWN HAS A WOLF.` → `GUBBIO, BEHIND ITS WALLS.` → `FRANCIS WALKS OUT.`

segments.voice: Francis is remembered as a merchant's son who gave away everything. In his Canticle of the Creatures he calls the sun his brother and the moon his sister, and the stories say he preached to birds. This one comes from the Little Flowers of Saint Francis, a collection of tales about him and his companions, written down after his time: a story told about him, the way families tell stories about a grandparent. A fierce wolf is killing animals, and even people, around Gubbio. Francis goes out to meet it. The wolf rushes at him with open jaws. Francis makes the sign of the cross and says, come here, Brother Wolf, and tells it, in Christ's name, not to hurt him or anyone. The wolf closes its mouth and lies down at his feet. Now watch what Francis does. He doesn't only scold the wolf. He names what it's done, and then why: it was hungry. So he makes a deal with both sides. The town will feed the wolf every day, and the wolf will harm no one again. The story says the wolf lifted its paw and put it in Francis's hand as a pledge, right there in the town square, in front of everyone. For two years after, it went from door to door and was fed, and the dogs didn't even bark at it. When it died of old age, the town grieved. Brother wolf: not a monster to kill, and not a pet either. A hungry creature, and a town that could afford to feed it. Peace asked something of everyone.
screen: `FRANCIS, WHO GAVE UP EVERYTHING.` · `COME HERE, BROTHER WOLF.` · `IT WAS HUNGRY.` · `A PAW IN HIS HAND.` · then, large: `BROTHER WOLF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a wild creature near where you live, a bird you might set water out for, a squirrel or a crow you could watch without shooing, and picture it clearly. Then think of your wolf, a person who bites. Without excusing anything, ask what they might be hungry for, and picture offering one small piece of it.
Francis. The saint who walked out to meet a killer, saw that it was hungry, and made a peace that fed it. Today's word.
Your line: brother wolf. Peace began with asking what the wolf was hungry for. Day eighty-nine, done.

90.title: Pascal's night of fire
90.hook: on 23 November 1654, Pascal writes two hours of fire on paper and sews it into his coat (the Memorial)
90.howItsDone: Christians who read Pascal treasure the Memorial as the record of his encounter with God; some people keep a copy of it, or a line of their own, close at hand in the same spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis, who saw the hunger behind the harm. Your line was brother wolf.

Is there something you keep close without telling anyone? A note from someone who's gone, folded in your wallet. A screenshot you never delete. A ticket stub in a drawer. The kind of thing people say they'd run back into a burning house for. Back on day ten we met Blaise Pascal, who said our unhappiness comes from not being able to sit quietly in a room. Today: what happened to him one night, alone in his own room, and what, the story goes, he carried in his coat from then on.
screen: `A NOTE IN YOUR WALLET.` → `PASCAL, BACK FROM DAY TEN.` → `ONE NIGHT, ALONE IN HIS ROOM.`

segments.voice: Pascal was a mathematician and an inventor. On a Monday night, the twenty-third of November, 1654, something happened to him, from about half past ten until about half past midnight. We don't know exactly what. What we have is what he wrote down right then, on a sheet of paper. It starts with a date and a time. Then one word, in capital letters: fire. Then he wrote that the God he met that night was the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, not the God of the philosophers and the scholars. This from a philosopher and scholar. Then, in broken lines, like someone out of breath: certainty; feeling; joy; peace. The word joy three times over, and tears of joy. He never published it, and as far as we know he never spoke of it. The story told after his death is that a servant felt something stiff in the lining of his coat and found the page sewn there, and that he had moved it by hand each time he changed coats. It's called the Memorial. For Pascal it was a meeting with God, the heart of his Christian faith. For anyone, it's a picture of how to treat the few moments that matter most: not as content to post, but as something to keep close.
screen: `A MATHEMATICIAN AND INVENTOR.` · `23 NOVEMBER 1654: FIRE.` · `NOT THE GOD OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.` · `SEWN INTO HIS COAT.` · then, large: `KEEP IT CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Think back over your life for a moment that mattered: a night, a sentence someone said, a place where something became clear; not the most dramatic, the truest. Find the fewest words that hold it, maybe just a date and one word, like Pascal's. If you like, write it on a small piece of paper and keep it somewhere close: a wallet, a pocket, a phone case.
Pascal. Two hours in 1654 that he wrote on a single page, sewed into his coat, and carried unseen until he died. Today's word.
Your line: keep it close. Not everything that matters has to be shown. Ninety days now.

screen: `DAY 90 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THOREAU GOES TO THE WOODS.`

91.title: Thoreau goes to the woods
91.hook: on 4 July 1845 he moves to Walden Pond to live deliberately and front the essential facts (Walden, chapter 2)
91.howItsDone: Readers of Walden often take up Thoreau's experiment in small ways: a simpler season, a walk without a phone, or asking of one habit whether it is chosen or just drifted into.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascal, and the page sewn into his coat. Your line was keep it close.

Look back at this week of ordinary saints. Socrates talking on his last day, admitting what he didn't know. Brother Lawrence at the sink. Julian with the world in her palm. Francis walking out to a wolf. Pascal's coat with its secret page. None of them were kings. All of them paid attention. The week ends in America, on Independence Day, 1845, with a young man moving his few belongings into a tiny cabin he'd built himself beside a pond.
screen: `A WEEK OF ORDINARY SAINTS.` → `NONE OF THEM KINGS.` → `A CABIN BY A POND, 1845.`

segments.voice: Henry David Thoreau built his cabin on the shore of Walden Pond, near Concord, Massachusetts. One room, a bed, a desk, three chairs. He wrote down exactly what it cost: twenty-eight dollars and twelve and a half cents. He lived there, as he says, two years and two months. In his book Walden he explained why: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived." Deliberately. On purpose. Not by default, not by habit, not because everyone else did it that way. Now the honest part. Walden wasn't the wilderness. The cabin was a short walk from town. Thoreau went into Concord often, had visitors, and ate meals with family and friends. People point that out as if it spoils the story. It doesn't. The point was never to vanish; it was to strip life down far enough to see what it's made of. Then he left, saying he had several more lives to live. So the experiment wasn't the cabin. It was the question he took there: am I choosing this, or just drifting through it? You don't need a pond to ask it. It fits the next hour just as well.
screen: `A CABIN BY WALDEN POND.` · `$28.12½, TWO YEARS, TWO MONTHS.` · `TO LIVE DELIBERATELY.` · `NOT A HERMIT, AN EXPERIMENT.` · then, large: `DELIBERATELY.`

segments.voice: Choose one small thing you'll do in the next hour anyway, drinking a glass of water, walking to the door, making a call, and picture doing it on purpose, start to finish. Notice the choice to begin, each part as it happens, and the moment you finish: nothing extra, just awake for the whole thing. When your mind drifts, notice that too, and come back.
Thoreau. Two years by a pond, near enough to town, to live deliberately and see what life is made of. Today's word.
Your line: deliberately. A life chosen on purpose, not just drifted into. That's day ninety-one.

fork.setup: you're Thoreau, young and restless in town. what do you do?
options: sail to Europe to see the world
build a small cabin by a pond and live simply
take a steady job and settle down
fork.reveal: he builds a one-room cabin at Walden Pond and moves in on July 4, 1845, to live deliberately and see what life is made of.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man who ran away to live in the woods.
what it means: a two-year experiment in choosing each part of life on purpose.
what a scholar hears: Walden, chapter 2, 'Where I Lived, and What I Lived For', where he went to front only the essential facts of life.
